overview: Tla’amin people live on the northern Sunshine Coast of British Columbia, with longstanding relationships across its lands and waters. The name of the main community, t̓išosəm, recalls waters whitened by herring spawn. Marine knowledge, family responsibilities and self-government remain central to the Nation’s life.

periods.title: Negotiating a modern treaty
periods.summary: Tla’amin entered the treaty process in 1994. Agreements with the provincial and federal governments culminated in signing in 2014, before the treaty took effect.

periods.title: Self-government under the treaty
periods.summary: The treaty took effect on April 5, 2016. The Nation describes this as a return to self-government, not the creation of Tla’amin identity or its first relationship with the land.

periods.title: Language renewal continues
periods.summary: The Nation adopted a new language revitalisation strategy in September 2025. Teaching and cultural work continue alongside governance, services and heritage protection.

sections.title: Building with tides and fish in mind

items.text: Stone fish traps on the Sliammon shoreline include semicircular enclosures. In Desolation Sound, some walls enhanced natural pools, holding fish as the tide receded. These surviving structures demonstrate deliberate modification of the shore around local water movement.

Other Desolation Sound traps used wooden stakes that supported barriers. Water preserved lower portions of the stakes after exposed wood disappeared. Archaeologists must reconstruct the working installation from these incomplete remains rather than treating what survives as its original height.

Trap designs could also combine stone or wooden guiding lines with removable woven baskets. Different structures served different settings and catches. Their variety reflects knowledge of fish movement as well as skill in construction.

Herring rakes were swept through schools of fish. Their teeth could be made from sharpened wood or bone, with iron nails used in more recent versions. The changing materials show an established harvesting method adapting to new supplies.
Fresh herring could be boiled or roasted, while smoking and sun-drying made it possible to store the catch. Preservation extended the value of a seasonal abundance beyond the day of fishing.

For roe collection, hemlock or cedar boughs were placed in the water during spawning. The eggs could be eaten fresh or dried. This used the fish’s spawning behaviour to obtain food without relying on the same tools as the fish harvest.

A Tla’amin-area research project combined trap mapping and archaeological sampling with community knowledge. Its researchers described studying old herring bones and their DNA to investigate abundance and diversity. Those methods ask about past fisheries; they do not by themselves establish the result.

The Nation describes kinship as a basis for rights, responsibilities and mutual support across villages. Elders transmit teachings through stories, instruction and example. Family relationships connect practical care with knowledge of territory.

Ancestral names are held by families and passed on with responsibilities. Naming and memorial gatherings affirm relationships and obligations. In the Nation’s account, ceremony is part of governance, rather than an activity detached from public life.

Tla’amin’s contemporary service model draws on making and caring for a baby basket. Preparation, weaving and maintenance provide ways to think about coordinated care and responsibility. Craft knowledge becomes a guide for designing present-day community services.

Language work includes workshops, recordings and resources for citizens living away from Tla’amin lands. Cultural staff also support heritage protection and repatriation inquiries. Keeping knowledge in circulation involves families, teachers, archives and community institutions.

On September 3, 2025, the Executive Council adopted a five-year strategy for ʔayʔaǰuθəm revitalisation. Its stated purpose is to strengthen the language’s presence in community life. Adopting a plan is a documented action, not proof that all its aims have been achieved.

ending.text: Colonial dispossession and the removal of children disrupted Tla’amin life. The Nation continues to rebuild services, cultural transmission and relationships with its territory. Its treaty took effect in 2016, restoring self-government within a new relationship with Canada and British Columbia; Tla’amin history continues.
